solution.concept_anchor: CRR and SLR share NDTL as common computational base
solution.strong_distractor: a — Pairing CRR with 'Total Assets' sounds authoritative since CRR is often described in terms of total bank liabilities loosely, and students unfamiliar with NDTL's precise definition may accept it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): CRR is calculated as a percentage of NDTL, not total assets. Total assets is a balance sheet measure; NDTL is a liability-side measure. The two are fundamentally different bases.
Eliminate (b): SLR is not computed as a percentage of net worth (equity capital). Net worth represents bank capital; SLR is a liability-side requirement based on NDTL.
Eliminate (d): The money multiplier is the inverse of CRR (simplified), not SLR. Pairing the money multiplier formula with SLR is an entity-swap error.
Confirm (c): Both CRR and SLR are computed as a percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) — this shared computational base is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) pairs SLR with the money multiplier formula (1/X), substituting SLR for CRR. A student who broadly knows both CRR and SLR affect credit and that there is a multiplier formula may not recall that the simplified multiplier uses CRR specifically, leading them to accept option (d) as a plausible match.
solution.final_explanation:
CRR and SLR share the same computational base — NDTL — which is the single most important definitional anchor for both ratios.

• Option (a) — Incorrectly matched: CRR is computed as a percentage of NDTL, not total assets. Total assets include all resources deployed (loans, investments, fixed assets), whereas NDTL is a liability-side concept.
• Option (b) — Incorrectly matched: SLR is not computed on net worth. Net worth is a capital concept (assets minus liabilities); SLR is computed on NDTL, a liability-side measure.
• Option (c) — Correctly matched: Both CRR and SLR are expressed as a percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities. NDTL includes demand deposits (savings, current accounts) and time deposits (FDs, RDs), net of inter-bank liabilities.
• Option (d) — Incorrectly matched: The simplified money multiplier formula uses CRR (1/CRR), not SLR. Substituting SLR is an entity-swap error.

Value Addition:
• NDTL data is published by the RBI weekly and is used as the base for computing CRR and SLR obligations each fortnight.
• The 'Net' in NDTL means inter-bank liabilities are excluded to prevent double-counting across the banking system.
• Demand liabilities include savings/current accounts; time liabilities include FDs and recurring deposits.

solution.concept_anchor: PACS exempt — UCB covered — RRB rate may differ from SCB

statement_analysis.statement: Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are required to maintain SLR under the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act and are subject to the same regulatory framework as scheduled commercial banks for this purpose.
statement_analysis.reason: UCBs are covered under the BR Act's SLR provisions. While their overall regulatory treatment has historically differed from SCBs, they are not exempt from SLR.

statement_analysis.statement: Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) are exempt from both CRR and SLR requirements because they are not classified as banks under the Banking Regulation Act.
statement_analysis.reason: PACS function as the grassroots tier of cooperative credit and are not regulated as banks under the BR Act; they fall outside the CRR and SLR framework entirely.

statement_analysis.statement: Regional Rural Banks are required to maintain SLR at the same rate as prescribed for scheduled commercial banks, with no provision for differential rates applicable to RRBs.
statement_analysis.reason: RRBs may be prescribed a different SLR rate by RBI/NABARD, reflecting their special developmental mandate and rural credit focus. The statement's claim of 'no provision for differential rates' is incorrect.

solution.strong_distractor: b — A student who knows PACS are exempt may mistakenly think Statement 2 is the one NOT correct (confusing it with District Central Cooperative Banks which do maintain SLR), choosing option (b) incorrectly.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — UCBs are covered under SLR provisions of the BR Act.
Statement 2 is correct — PACS are explicitly outside the CRR/SLR framework because they are not banks under the BR Act.
Statement 3 is NOT correct — RRBs may face differential SLR rates prescribed by RBI/NABARD; the statement's denial of any differential provision is the factual error.
Only Statement 3 is NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses the 'scope-extension' technique — adding 'with no provision for differential rates applicable to RRBs' to what would otherwise be a partially true statement. Students who know RRBs maintain SLR but haven't specifically studied whether differential rates are permissible may accept Statement 3 as true, making it the hardest statement to flag as incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
Cooperative institutions span multiple regulatory tiers, and precise knowledge of which tier maintains what requirement is a perennial UPSC testing area.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Urban Cooperative Banks are within the SLR framework under the Banking Regulation Act. They are regulated as banking entities and bear SLR obligations accordingly.
• Statement 2 — Correct: PACS are explicitly exempt from CRR and SLR. They are the lowest tier of cooperative credit — member-owned societies that lend to farmers — and are not governed as banks under the BR Act.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect (the NOT correct statement): RRBs are permitted differential SLR rates. Their unique developmental mandate — providing rural and agricultural credit — allows RBI and NABARD to prescribe a rate different from that applicable to mainstream SCBs. The categorical denial of 'any provision for differential rates' is the false element.

Value Addition:
• District Central Cooperative Banks and State Cooperative Banks — above PACS in the cooperative hierarchy — do maintain SLR.
• RRBs are sponsored by commercial banks but have distinct CRR/SLR prescription authority resting with RBI/NABARD.
• UCBs were brought under closer RBI supervision post-2020 amendments to the BR Act.

solution.concept_anchor: HTM exemption protects bank balance sheets during rate hike cycles
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both facts about rising rates reducing bond prices (A) and HTM exemption protecting banks (R) may assume R directly explains A, when in fact A is a general market phenomenon and R is a bank-specific accounting response — R explains the bank's protection, not why bond prices fall.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? Yes — bond prices and interest rates move inversely; rising interest rates reduce the market value of existing fixed-coupon bonds.

Step 2: Is R correct? Yes — banks can classify SLR securities under HTM, which exempts them from mark-to-market valuation; HTM securities are carried at acquisition cost regardless of market price movements.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? No — A states a general financial market fact (interest rates and bond prices move inversely). R explains the accounting treatment that protects banks from the impact of this fact, not the underlying reason why bond prices fall. The causal explanation of A (inverse bond price-rate relationship) is the mathematics of discounted cash flow pricing, not the HTM rule. R is a consequence of A (i.e., because A is true, R matters), not an explanation of A.
solution.final_explanation:
The inverse relationship between bond prices and interest rates (A) is a fundamental market pricing principle. The HTM exemption (R) is a regulatory/accounting response to manage the consequences of that principle for banks — not an explanation of it.

• Assertion (A): Correct. When prevailing interest rates rise, existing fixed-coupon bonds become less attractive. Their prices fall in the secondary market to align their yield with the new higher rates. This is basic bond mathematics (discounted cash flow pricing).
• Reason (R): Correct. Under HTM classification permitted by RBI for SLR securities, banks carry those securities at acquisition (book) cost. Market price declines due to rate hikes do not flow through to the Profit and Loss account as unrealised losses.
• Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. A is explained by bond pricing mathematics (discounted cash flow). R is the banking sector's accounting response to A — a way of managing the impact of A — not its underlying cause. Therefore, both are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A — option (b).

Value Addition:
• Banks holding large HFT (Held-for-Trading) portfolios take immediate MTM losses during rate hike cycles — making HTM classification strategically valuable.
• RBI's HTM ceiling for SLR securities is periodically revised upward during volatile rate environments to provide accounting relief.
• The 2022–23 rate hike cycle in India (and globally) made the HTM-SLR relationship extremely relevant for banking sector analysis.

solution.concept_anchor: Financial repression, Narasimham, crowding-out — CRR/SLR policy history
solution.strong_distractor: b — Swapping the descriptions of 'financial repression' (List II item 2) and 'crowding out' (List II item 4) is the planned trap, as students know both concepts relate to mandatory G-sec holdings without distinguishing which label applies where.
elimination_logic: A (Narasimham Committee I, 1991) → 3 (recommended CRR/SLR reduction for financial liberalisation): This is the most anchored match — Narasimham I's core CRR/SLR recommendation.

B (High SLR redirecting bank funds to government at below-market rates) → 2 (financial repression): 'Financial repression' is specifically defined as policy forcing banks to lend to government at below-market rates.
C (SLR reducing resources available for private sector credit) → 4 (crowding out of private credit): Crowding out is the displacement of private credit by mandatory government lending.

D (CRR raising banks' cost of funds transmitted as higher lending rates) → 1 (raises effective cost of financial intermediation): Higher CRR means higher average cost per rupee lent — this is the intermediation cost mechanism. Correct: A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1 → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is swapping 'financial repression' and 'crowding out' — B and C. Both relate to mandatory G-sec holdings, but financial repression specifically implies below-market-rate lending to the government (an exploitative element), while crowding out simply describes the resource displacement (a mechanical outcome). Students who use the two terms interchangeably — treating mandatory G-sec holdings as 'either financial repression or crowding out' without distinguishing which applies to below-market rates — will swap B-2 and C-4.
solution.final_explanation:
The policy critique of high CRR and SLR operates through multiple channels — intermediation cost, resource displacement, and institutional terms-of-trade — each with a precise label.

Correct matches: A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1
• A (Narasimham Committee I, 1991) — 3: Narasimham I recommended CRR reduction to 3–5% and SLR to 25% as the cornerstone of financial liberalisation — the most historically significant CRR/SLR reform recommendation.
• B (SLR forcing banks to lend to government at below-market rates) — 2: This is the textbook definition of 'financial repression' — mandatory lending to the government at rates below what the free market would set.
• C (SLR reducing resources for private credit) — 4: 'Crowding out' is the displacement of private sector credit when banks are compelled to allocate resources to government instruments.
• D (High CRR raising cost of funds, transmitted as higher lending rates) — 1: This describes the cost-of-intermediation channel — banks compensate for the zero-return CRR burden by charging borrowers higher interest rates.

Value Addition:
• Financial repression and crowding out co-exist when SLR is high — they are not mutually exclusive.
• The Narasimham Committee used both the financial repression and crowding-out arguments to justify pre-emption reduction.
• Current CRR + SLR ≈ 22% — versus over 53% at the 1991 peak.

solution.concept_anchor: CRR floor/ceiling removal — Finance Act 2006, not 1991

statement_analysis.statement: Prior to the Finance Act of 2006, the Cash Reserve Ratio was subject to a statutory floor of 3% and a ceiling of 20%, and the Reserve Bank of India could only prescribe rates within this band.
statement_analysis.reason: Before the Finance Act 2006 amended the RBI Act, Section 42(1) did prescribe a 3% minimum and 20% maximum for CRR, within which the RBI could exercise discretion.

statement_analysis.statement: The removal of statutory limits on CRR was implemented through the Banking Regulation Act (Amendment) Act, 1991, as part of the financial sector reforms recommended by the Narasimham Committee.
statement_analysis.reason: The statutory limits on CRR were removed by the Finance Act, 2006 — not through any 1991 amendment to the Banking Regulation Act. The 1991 reforms were recommendations; legislative removal of CRR limits came 15 years later.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Narasimham 1991 recommended CRR deregulation and know limits were eventually removed may conflate the recommendation year with the implementation legislation year.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — the pre-2006 CRR band of 3% floor and 20% ceiling is accurately described.
Statement 2 is incorrect — it wrongly attributes the removal to a 1991 BR Act amendment; the actual removal was through the Finance Act 2006, and it amended the RBI Act (not the BR Act).
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, the answer is option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a double trap: wrong year (1991 instead of 2006) and wrong statute (Banking Regulation Act instead of the Finance Act amending the RBI Act). A student who remembers only that '1991 started CRR liberalisation' and does not recall that the actual legal change came in 2006 through a Finance Act amendment will accept Statement 2 as true, choosing option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The legislative history of CRR limit removal is a precision-testing point — the recommendation and the implementation are separated by 15 years and different legislative instruments.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Prior to 2006, CRR was constrained by a statutory floor (3%) and ceiling (20%) embedded in Section 42(1) of the RBI Act. The RBI could only vary CRR within this legislatively fixed band.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Two errors are present. First, the removal was effected through the Finance Act, 2006 — not a 1991 amendment. Second, it was the RBI Act that was amended, not the Banking Regulation Act (which governs SLR, not CRR). The 1991 Narasimham Committee made the recommendation; legislative action followed only in 2006.

Value Addition:
• The Finance Act (not a standalone banking law) is the vehicle that amended the RBI Act's CRR provisions — an important procedural detail.
• SLR limits (0% floor, 40% ceiling) in the BR Act were NOT removed in 2006 and remain in force.
• Post-2006, the RBI has kept CRR at levels between 3% and 9% — well within the old band in practice, even though the statutory constraint no longer exists.

solution.concept_anchor: LCR vs SLR — functionally similar, structurally different asset definitions
solution.strong_distractor: c — Stating that LCR and SLR are entirely unrelated and serve no common purpose sounds precise but is wrong; the two do share a functional similarity in ensuring liquidity buffers.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b): SLR is not a Basel III requirement; it is an India-specific statutory requirement under the BR Act predating Basel III.
Eliminate (c): LCR and SLR are not entirely unrelated — both aim at ensuring banks hold liquid assets sufficient to survive a specified stress period or meet regulatory minima.

Eliminate (d): LCR eligible assets under Basel III are broader than SLR-eligible assets; corporate bonds (high-quality) qualify under LCR but not SLR — the statement in (d) that LCR has a narrower asset definition is incorrect.

Confirm (a): LCR and SLR share the functional objective of ensuring banks hold liquid assets, but differ in asset definition (LCR accepts certain corporate bonds; SLR restricts to sovereign instruments) and regulatory framework (Basel III vs BR Act).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) is a conflation trap that swaps the relative breadth of LCR and SLR asset definitions. LCR has a broader eligible asset universe (includes High-Quality Liquid Assets like some corporate bonds), while SLR is narrower (restricted to sovereign/quasi-sovereign). Students who associate LCR with 'RBI-specific, more conservative' may mistakenly believe SLR has the broader definition.
solution.final_explanation:
Both LCR and SLR are liquidity buffer requirements but arise from different regulatory traditions and define eligible assets differently.

• Option (a) — Correct: LCR (Liquidity Coverage Ratio under Basel III) and SLR both require banks to hold liquid assets. However, LCR accepts a broader set of High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA), including some corporate bonds and covered bonds, while SLR restricts eligible assets to gold, cash, and sovereign instruments (G-secs, T-bills, SDLs). Their frameworks — international Basel III vs India's BR Act — are also distinct.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: SLR is not a Basel III instrument. It pre-dates Basel III and is an India-specific statutory requirement. India's LCR compliance is separate from and in addition to SLR.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: LCR and SLR are functionally related — both address the same core concern (bank liquidity during stressed conditions). Calling them 'entirely unrelated' overstates their differences.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: LCR has a broader, not narrower, asset definition than SLR. G-secs held for SLR count toward LCR HQLA, but LCR additionally accepts instruments SLR does not.

Value Addition:
• India's SLR partially satisfies LCR requirements since G-secs are HQLA Level 1 under Basel III.
• NSFR (Net Stable Funding Ratio) is another Basel III metric addressing longer-term structural liquidity — distinct from both SLR and LCR.
• Banks must comply with both SLR (BR Act) and LCR (RBI Basel III guidelines) simultaneously.

solution.concept_anchor: CRR shortfall penal rate — Bank Rate + 3% first day, Bank Rate + 5% subsequent days
solution.strong_distractor: b — Choosing 'repo rate plus a penalty' sounds technically correct because the repo rate is the most prominent RBI rate students encounter. The use of Bank Rate (not repo rate) as the base is a precision trap.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): A blanket suspension of lending rights is not the prescribed regulatory consequence for CRR shortfall; the BR Act and RBI Act provide for penal interest, not lending restrictions.

Eliminate (b): The penal rate is based on the Bank Rate (not the repo rate). These are distinct rates; confusing them is the core trap. Bank Rate is the rate at which RBI lends to banks without collateral — distinct from the collateralised repo rate.
Eliminate (d): The Reserve Bank Act does not prescribe a fixed penalty of ₹500 per lakh — penal consequences are interest-based, not a fixed per-unit fee.
Confirm (c): CRR shortfall attracts penal interest at Bank Rate plus 3 percentage points for the first day and Bank Rate plus 5 percentage points for each subsequent day of continued non-compliance.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) substitutes 'repo rate' for 'Bank Rate' — a precise entity-swap within the same RBI rate family. Both repo rate and Bank Rate are RBI-prescribed rates, but the penal CRR rate formula specifically uses the Bank Rate. Students who associate all penal rate computations with the repo rate (the most discussed RBI rate) will choose option (b) with confidence.
solution.final_explanation:
CRR compliance is monitored daily, and shortfalls are penalised through an interest-rate-based mechanism using the Bank Rate as the reference — not the policy repo rate.

In the scenario, the bank's CRR balance falls below 90% of the required level on consecutive days. The applicable regulatory consequence is:

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Suspension of lending operations is not prescribed. Regulatory action for CRR shortfall is financial (penal interest), not operational.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The penal rate is based on the Bank Rate, not the policy repo rate. Though both are RBI-set rates, they serve different functions. Using 'repo rate' is the planted precision error.
• Option (c) — Correct: Bank Rate + 3% applies for the first day of CRR shortfall; Bank Rate + 5% for each subsequent day of continued non-compliance. This graduated penalty is designed to incentivise prompt correction.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: A fixed per-unit monetary penalty is not prescribed in the CRR enforcement mechanism. The consequence is interest-based, scaling with the amount of shortfall and duration.

Value Addition:
• The Bank Rate in India is currently set at 25 basis points above the MSF rate.
• The graduated penal structure (3% → 5%) encourages banks to correct shortfalls within the first day.
• CRR shortfall data is not publicly disclosed per individual bank but aggregate shortfall statistics appear in RBI publications.

solution.concept_anchor: CRR maintenance location, SLR asset custody, NDTL netting

statement_analysis.statement: CRR balances are maintained by banks as cash deposited with the Reserve Bank of India, and physical cash kept in bank vaults or ATMs does not count toward the CRR requirement.
statement_analysis.reason: CRR is specifically maintained as cash balances with the RBI through the current account maintained by each scheduled commercial bank; vault cash is not counted.

statement_analysis.statement: SLR assets are held on the books of the bank itself — not deposited with the RBI — making the bank the custodian of its own SLR portfolio.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike CRR, SLR securities (G-secs, T-bills, gold, etc.) remain on the bank's own balance sheet and are managed by the bank's treasury department.

statement_analysis.statement: Inter-bank borrowings and deposits are included in NDTL at their gross value to ensure the regulator captures the full extent of the banking system's liability exposure.
statement_analysis.reason: The 'Net' in NDTL specifically means inter-bank liabilities are excluded (netted out). Including them at gross value would cause double-counting of the same deposits across multiple banks.

statement_analysis.statement: Both CRR and SLR are calculated as a percentage of the same base — Net Demand and Time Liabilities — ensuring a consistent liability-side foundation for both reserve requirements.
statement_analysis.reason: NDTL is the common computational base for both CRR and SLR. This is explicitly prescribed in the RBI Act (for CRR) and the Banking Regulation Act (for SLR).

solution.strong_distractor: d — A student who confuses 'net' with 'net of SLR' (rather than 'net of inter-bank liabilities') in the NDTL definition may accept Statement 3 as correct, leading to 'all four' correct and choosing option (d).
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — CRR is held with RBI; vault cash does not count.
Statement 2 is correct — SLR assets are on the bank's own books, not with RBI.
Statement 3 is incorrect — inter-bank liabilities are NETTED OUT from NDTL; including them at gross value contradicts the 'Net' in NDTL.
Statement 4 is correct — NDTL is the shared base for both CRR and SLR; three of four are correct → option (a) only one is wrong → 'Only three' are correct → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 sounds regulatory-minded and comprehensive — 'capturing full liability exposure' sounds like something regulators would want. The trap is that 'full gross capture' would cause double-counting: a deposit Bank A holds with Bank B would add to both banks' NDTL, inflating aggregate reserve requirements artificially. The 'Net' in NDTL exists precisely to prevent this.
solution.final_explanation:
The mechanics of CRR and SLR — where assets are held, what base is used, and how inter-bank exposures are treated — form a cluster of frequently tested precision points.

• Statement 1 — Correct: CRR = cash balances with RBI only. Vault cash, ATM cash, and cash in transit do not count. Each bank maintains a current account with the RBI for this purpose.
• Statement 2 — Correct: SLR assets stay on the bank's balance sheet. The bank's treasury manages G-secs, T-bills, SDLs, and gold — they are not transferred to the RBI.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Inter-bank deposits and borrowings are netted out in computing NDTL. The 'Net' prefix is the defining feature. Gross inclusion would double-count the same underlying funds across the banking system.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Both CRR (RBI Act, Section 42) and SLR (BR Act, Section 24) use NDTL as the denominator — providing regulatory consistency and comparability.

Value Addition:
• Banks maintain current accounts with RBI's regional offices — these current account balances = CRR.
• Gold is an SLR-eligible asset — valued at current market prices for SLR computation purposes.
• NDTL computation is done fortnightly and reported to the RBI for CRR and SLR assessment.

solution.concept_anchor: LAF corridor — repo, reverse repo/SDF, MSF rate positions
solution.strong_distractor: a — Swapping the positions of the repo rate and MSF rate in the LAF corridor is the core confusion: placing MSF rate as the 'middle' and repo rate as the 'ceiling' inverts the actual structure.
elimination_logic: A (Standing Deposit Facility rate) → 4: SDF rate forms the floor of the LAF corridor — banks park excess funds with RBI at this rate (introduced in 2022 replacing the fixed-rate reverse repo as corridor floor).
B (Policy Repo Rate) → 2: Repo rate is the middle benchmark of the LAF corridor — banks borrow from RBI at this rate against collateral.
C (MSF Rate) → 1: MSF rate is above the repo rate — it forms the ceiling of the LAF corridor, accessible for emergency overnight borrowing.

D (Temporary dip in SLR by up to 2% of NDTL) → 3: This is precisely the defining feature of MSF — banks can access funds by temporarily breaching SLR by up to 2% of NDTL. Correct: A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3 → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in option (a) which swaps SDF and MSF positions — placing SDF at the ceiling and MSF at the floor. Students who know the LAF has a floor and ceiling but have not memorised which rate corresponds to which position will confuse SDF (floor) and MSF (ceiling). The mnemonic to retain: SDF is where banks park funds at the lowest rate (floor); MSF is where banks borrow at the highest rate (ceiling).
solution.final_explanation:
The LAF corridor is structured as a three-rate band with the policy repo rate at the centre, flanked by the SDF rate (floor) and MSF rate (ceiling).

Correct matches: A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3
• A (Standing Deposit Facility Rate) — 4 (Floor of LAF corridor): Since April 2022, the SDF rate replaced the fixed-rate reverse repo as the corridor floor. Banks park excess funds with RBI at this rate — the lowest in the corridor.
• B (Policy Repo Rate) — 2 (Middle benchmark of LAF corridor): Banks borrow from RBI against G-sec collateral at the repo rate — the main policy signal of the monetary stance.
• C (MSF Rate) — 1 (Ceiling of LAF corridor): MSF rate = Repo rate + 25 bps. It is the highest rate in the corridor; banks access it only under acute liquidity stress.
• D (Temporary SLR dip up to 2% of NDTL) — 3 (Defining feature of MSF access): Under MSF, banks can borrow overnight by temporarily reducing their SLR below the mandatory minimum by up to 2% of NDTL.

Value Addition:
• Pre-April 2022, the reverse repo rate formed the corridor floor; it has since been replaced by the SDF rate.
• The LAF corridor width (SDF to MSF) is typically 50 bps in India — 25 bps on each side of the repo rate.
• MSF borrowing is available on all days (including weekends) unlike the standard repo window.
